 1                          I.         INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state for the record your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Courtney Fieldman. I am the Utility Program director at the

 4        Southwest Energy Efficiency Project (“SWEEP”). My business address is

 5        2334 Broadway, Suite A, Boulder, Colorado 80304.

 6   Q.   Have you previously filed testimony in this case?

 7   A.   Yes. I previously filed direct testimony on behalf of Coalition for Clean

 8        Affordable Energy (“CCAE”) on October 23, 2026.

 9   Q.   What is the purpose of your rebuttal testimony?

10   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to the positions of other

11        parties regarding the residential customer charge and El Paso Electric

12        Company’s (“EPE”) proposed Low-Income Rider (“LIR”). I respond to

13        City of Las Cruces (“CLC”) Witness Justin R. Barnes; Utility Division Staff

14        (“Staff”) Witnesses Richard J. Bunch, Douglas B. Jester, and Christopher

15        E. Dunn; and New Mexico Department of Justice (“DOJ”) Witnesses Jamal

16        Mamkhezri and Doug Gegax. My rebuttal testimony supports five

17        positions.



                                           1
          Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                           Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1           First, the residential customer charge should be no higher than $8.88

 2   per month. A fixed monthly charge should recover only the cost of

 3   connecting a customer to the system and keeping that customer connected.

 4   The charges recommended by Staff and DOJ are lower than EPE’s proposal,

 5   but each would still recover usage- and demand-related costs through a

 6   charge that customers cannot reduce by using less electricity, which raises

 7   bills most for the customers who use the least.

 8           Second, the cost of the LIR should be paid by all customer classes.

 9   Low-income rate relief carries out a policy the Legislature adopted for the

10   State as a whole, and it benefits the entire system by reducing unpaid bills.

11   DOJ’s recommendation to charge the cost only to other residential

12   customers would require struggling households that are not enrolled to pay

13   for the credits of those that are.

14           Third, the LIR should reach the households it is meant to serve.

15   Limiting eligibility to LIHEAP recipients, as Staff recommends, or to

16   LIHEAP and SNAP recipients, as DOJ recommends, would leave out most

17   income-qualified households. The Commission should instead accept

18   participation in any of the programs it has already approved for identifying

                                          2
                    Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                      Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             low-income customers, including the process used in the Community Solar

 2             low-income eligibility and the transportation electrification plans, and

 3             accept self-attestation.

 4                        Fourth, the low-income credit should be a stand-alone amount sized

 5             to the bill increase that participating households will face, not an amount

 6             tied to the amount of the customer charge.

 7                        Fifth, the LIR should be adopted as a permanent rate rather than a

 8             pilot, and its effectiveness should be evaluated in EPE’s next general rate

 9             case.

10                  II.          RESPONSES TO DIRECT TESTIMONY

11        a.       Response to CLC Witness Justin R. Barnes

12   Q.        Have you reviewed the direct testimony of Justin R. Barnes on behalf

13             of the City of Las Cruces?

14   A.        Yes. I agree with Mr. Barnes’ recommended exclusions and adjustments to

15             expenses improperly included in EPE’s proposed residential customer

16             charge. 1 In my Direct Testimony I discussed why FERC Account 369 is not




     1
               Justin R. Barnes Direct Test. at 30:5–31:9 (Oct. 23, 2026).
                                                   3
                 Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                 Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1          properly included in the customer charge. Therefore, I recommend one

 2          additional exclusion for FERC Account 369, Services, consistent with my

 3          direct testimony.

 4                 I also agree with Mr. Barnes that the costs of low-income rate relief

 5          should be allocated among all customer classes and collected by using a

 6          tariff. 2 For the reasons I explain in response to DOJ Witness Mamkhezri,

 7          this is the appropriate way to recover a cost incurred to carry out a statewide

 8          policy objective that benefits EPE’s entire system.

 9                 However, I do not agree with Mr. Barnes's recommendation to limit

10          the low-income discount to 50% of the residential customer charge, or to tie

11          the credit amount to the residential customer charge. 3 As explained in my

12          direct testimony, the amount of the low-income credit should be determined

13          by the need to provide meaningful rate relief, not by the amount of the

14          customer charge.

15   Q.     What customer charge results from Mr. Barnes’s adjustments?


     2
            Id. at 7:2–4, 22:14–16. Staff Witness Jester similarly recommends that the
     revenue lost to the LIR be recovered from all customer classes in proportion to
     revenue. Douglas Jester Direct Test. at 69:19–20 (Oct. 23, 2026).
     3
            Barnes Direct at 34:11–21.
                                              4
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                 Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   A.   Mr. Barnes calculates a $10.95 monthly residential customer charge. 4 I

 2        support these adjustments for the same reason I stated in my Direct

 3        Testimony. These are the types of charges that are not appropriately

 4        characterized as customer charges and should therefore not be charged and

 5        collected as fixed, customer charges.

 6   Q.   What additional adjustment do you recommend?

 7   A.   As I explained in my direct testimony, EPE should remove FERC Account

 8        369, Services, from the residential customer charge and classify those costs

 9        as distribution-related costs recovered through the energy charge. Account

10        369 includes service drops used to deliver electricity from the distribution

11        system to customer meters. Mr. Barnes’s Table 1 assigns $2.07 per

12        residential customer-month to Account 369, but his $10.95 calculation does

13        not deduct that amount. 5 Deducting the additional $2.07 produces a

14        residential customer charge of $8.88 per month. This is my recommended

15        charge using EPE’s cost-of-service assumptions as adjusted by Mr. Barnes

16        and by my additional Account 369 exclusion.


     4
          Id. at 24:10–25:1, tbls. 2–3.
     5
          Id. at 10:1, tbl. 1; id. at 25:1, tbl. 3.
                                                5
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                              Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q.   Do you agree with Mr. Barnes that all customers should pay the costs

 2        of low-income rates?

 3   A.   Yes. Mr. Barnes states that the costs of providing low-income rate relief is

 4        a public policy objective. 6 This is demonstrated by the legislature having

 5        authorized the Commission to adopt low-income rates. The public benefit

 6        should be paid for by all customer classes, rather than imposed exclusively

 7        on residential customers. Affordable access to essential electric service and

 8        reduced energy insecurity confers a net public benefit, and the cost of

 9        providing that benefit should be shared across EPE’s customer classes. I

10        recommend a low-income discount rate rider to recover the revenue

11        required for the approved bill credit, allocated among customer classes on

12        the revenue basis Mr. Barnes recommends. That cost should not be added

13        to the residential customer charge. Spreading the costs to all ratepayers

14        makes whatever low-income rate the Commission approves more

15        affordable and recognizes the system-wide benefits an LIR can provide.

16   Q.   Do you agree with Mr. Barnes recommendations to link the low-income



     6
          Id. at 22:14–16, 33:22–15.
                                            6
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1         credit amount to the customer charge?

2    A.   No. Mr. Barnes recommends an interim discount equal to 50% of the

 3        adopted residential customer charge. 7 His proposal would link the value of

 4        low-income assistance to a fixed customer charge, even though that charge

 5        does not measure a household’s energy burden or the increase in its overall

 6        bill. I continue to recommend a stand-alone monthly credit applicable to the

 7        entire bill, not tied or based on the amount of any particular bill component.

 8        In my direct testimony, I identified an inflation-adjusted $25 monthly credit

 9        as an alternative, but CCAE’s preferred recommendation is $55 per month

10        to offset EPE’s illustrated $55 non-fuel increase for a residential customer

11        using 750 kWh during a summer month, with the credit adjusted to reflect

12        the increase ultimately approved by the Commission.

13   Q.   Why do you disagree with limiting the credit to 50% of the customer

14        charge?

15   A.   The appropriate amount of assistance should be determined by the

16        affordability problem the Commission is trying to address, not by the size



     7
          Id. at 34:11–12.
                                            7
                    Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                   Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             of the fixed monthly customer charge. Moreover, the funding approach that

 2             Mr. Barnes recommends and that I support would distribute the cost among

 3             all customer classes rather than collecting it from nonparticipating

 4             residential customers. That approach mitigates the burden on the residential

 5             class. Future refinements to eligibility or program administration should be

 6             considered without limiting current assistance to the customer charge

 7             amount, which I recommend reducing.

 8        b.       Response to Staff Witness Richard J. Bunch

 9   Q.        What does Staff Witness Bunch recommend regarding LIR eligibility?

10   A.        Mr. Bunch recommends limiting eligibility for the LIR to customers who

11             receive assistance through the Low Income Home Energy Assistance

12             Program (“LIHEAP”). 8

13   Q.        Do you agree with Mr. Bunch’s recommendation to limit eligibility for

14             the LIR?

15   A.        No. Eligibility for the LIR should depend on whether a household is low-

16             income, and enrollment in LIHEAP is not a reliable measure of that status.



     8
               Richard J. Bunch Direct Test. at 16:10–15 (Oct. 23, 2026).
                                                8
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                              Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        LIHEAP is a limited, federally funded benefit. Whether a household

 2        receives LIHEAP assistance in a given year depends on whether the

 3        household applied for assistance and whether funds were available, rather

 4        than on whether the household’s income qualifies it for help. Limiting

 5        eligibility to LIHEAP recipients would therefore exclude most of the

 6        households the LIR is intended to serve.

 7        Staff’s own analysis demonstrates the extent of that gap. Mr. Bunch

 8        estimates that approximately 20,496 of EPE’s 98,354 New Mexico

 9        residential customers have incomes below the federal poverty level. 9 By

10        comparison, EPE identified 5,329 current LIHEAP recipients among its

11        New Mexico customers. 10 A program limited to LIHEAP recipients would

12        therefore reach, at most, approximately one in four of the households Staff

13        identifies as living below the poverty level. Mr. Bunch further reports that

14        approximately 19,592 households in Doña Ana County and 4,443

15        households in Otero County receive SNAP benefits. 11 EPE has



     9
          Id. at 10:9–11.
     10
          Manuel Carrasco Direct Test. Am. at 49:1–4 (Aug. 6, 2026).
     11
          Bunch Direct at 10:19–11:4.
                                           9
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        acknowledged that the eligible population would be larger once participants

 2        in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (“SNAP”) are

 3        included, 12 and its proposal already includes SNAP participants. Staff’s

 4        recommendation would therefore narrow eligibility below the level that

 5        EPE itself has proposed.

 6   Q.   What eligibility criteria do you recommend instead?

 7   A.   The Commission should qualify a customer for the LIR if the customer

 8        participates in any program on the list the Commission has already adopted

 9        in Rule 573, the Community Solar Rules, for identifying low-income

10        customers, and should allow a customer who does not participate in one of

11        those programs to qualify by self-attestation. The eligibility list in Rule 573

12        includes Medicaid; SNAP; LIHEAP; first-time homeowner and housing

13        rehabilitation programs; residence in a low-income or affordable housing

14        facility; and state and federal income tax credit programs. 13 The same rule

15        permits a customer to qualify by self-attestation. 14



     12
          Carrasco Direct Am. at 49:4–7.
     13
          17.9.573.15(A) NMAC (as amended Oct. 22, 2024).
     14
          Id. 17.9.573.15(C).
                                            10
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        I recommend this approach for three reasons. First, the Commission has

 2        already determined that participation in these programs is reliable evidence

 3        that a household is low-income, and a household the Commission treats as

 4        low-income under one of its rules should not be treated as ineligible for low-

 5        income rate relief from the same utility. Second, each of these programs

 6        already verifies household income or requires self-attestation, so EPE

 7        would not need to build a new income-verification process. Third, the list

 8        reaches the households the LIR is intended to serve, rather than only those

 9        that happened to receive a limited LIHEAP benefit.

10   Q.   Why does Mr. Bunch recommend excluding SNAP participants?

11   A.   Mr. Bunch recommends excluding SNAP because of concerns about data

12        sharing and customer privacy. 15 Mr. Bunch is concerned that the State may

13        be unwilling to share SNAP participant data with EPE, given that it recently

14        declined a federal request for SNAP cardholder data, and that SNAP

15        recipients reasonably expect that their participation will not be disclosed to

16        their utility.16


     15
          Bunch Direct 16:20–17:5.
     16
          Id. at 17:2–9.
                                           11
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                              Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q.   Do Mr. Bunch’s concerns regarding data sharing and customer privacy

 2        justify limiting eligibility to LIHEAP?

 3   A.   No. Mr. Bunch’s privacy concerns warrant careful design of the enrollment

 4        process, but they do not justify excluding eligible households from the

 5        program. Those concerns arise from EPE’s proposal to identify participants

 6        by matching its customer records against the State’s client database. If

 7        customers instead establish eligibility by presenting proof of their own

 8        enrollment or by self-attestation, the State would not need to transfer any

 9        SNAP records to EPE, and the decision whether to disclose program

10        participation would remain with the customer. The protections Mr. Bunch

11        describes, including limiting EPE’s access to the information needed to

12        determine eligibility and prohibiting any secondary use of that information,

13        can be applied to those enrollment methods without excluding any eligible

14        household. 17

15   Q.   Do you agree with Mr. Bunch’s recommendation that the LIR be




     17
          Bunch Direct at 18:5–22.
                                          12
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                              Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        approved as a pilot program?

 2   A.   No. I recommend that the Commission approve the LIR as a permanent rate

 3        and evaluate its effectiveness in EPE’s next general rate case. Mr. Bunch

 4        recommends that the LIR be treated initially as a pilot program, operated

 5        for two years without substantial change, and evaluated within 26 months

 6        after it begins. 18 I agree with Mr. Bunch that the Commission should

 7        evaluate the effectiveness of the program. However, designating the LIR as

 8        a pilot is neither necessary nor advisable. It is not necessary because the

 9        Legislature acted in authorizing the Commission to approve low-income

10        rates, not low-income rate pilots. Furthermore, it is not advisable because a

11        program presented to customers as temporary is likely to enroll fewer of the

12        households it is intended to serve. “Affordability” is a concern across the

13        country as utilities seek to serve new data center load, and New Mexico and

14        EPE are not exceptions.

15               The Public Utility Act now provides that its prohibition on rate

16        discrimination does not prevent the Commission from approving “rates and



     18
          Id. at 12:6–17, 20:13–20.
                                           13
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        programs designed to reduce the burden of energy costs on low-income

2         customers.” 19 Whether the Commission may approve a low-income rate for

3         EPE’s customers has therefore been settled as a matter of state policy. The

4         questions that remain concern the design of the program, including the level

5         of the credit, the methods of enrollment, and the cost of the program. These

6         are matters the Commission routinely examines in a general rate case, and

7         they do not require a pilot designation.

8                A pilot designation would also undermine the enrollment on which

9         the program’s success depends. EPE has acknowledged in discovery that it

10        would consider terminating the rider if participation considerably exceeds

11        its estimate. 20 Community organizations are less likely to invest in outreach,

12        and eligible households are less likely to enroll, when a program is

13        designated as temporary and the utility administering it has stated that it

14        may discontinue the program. An evaluation based on that diminished

15        enrollment would understate the program’s effectiveness and could lead the

16        Commission to draw inaccurate conclusions about its value.


     19
          NMSA § 62-8-6(C) (2025).
     20
          EPE Resp. to City of Las Cruces 4-6 (Ex. CF-3 at 4).
                                            14
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1                The Commission can obtain the evaluation Mr. Bunch recommends

 2        without designating the LIR as a pilot. The LIR, like every other EPE rate,

 3        will be subject to review in EPE’s next general rate case, and Mr. Bunch

 4        himself recommends that his proposed evaluation be incorporated into that

 5        case if EPE files within the evaluation period. 21 To support that review, I

 6        recommend that the Commission require EPE to file annual reports on

 7        program enrollment, credits provided, costs recovered from each customer

 8        class, and arrearage and disconnection rates among participants, and to

 9        present a comprehensive evaluation of the program in its next general rate

10        case. That record will provide the Commission with the information

11        necessary to adjust the credit level, eligibility criteria, or cost recovery

12        mechanism based on the program’s actual performance.

13   Q.   When should the low-income rate take effect?

14   A.   It should correspond to how the rate increase is phased in. If there is no

15        phase-in, the low-income credit should take effect in full when the rates go

16        into effect. If there is a phase-in, the credit may be phased in proportionately



     21
          Bunch Direct at 20:13–20.
                                            15
                    Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                   Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             to the rate increase so that the assistance corresponds to the additional

 2             charges that eligible households might face.

 3        c.       Response to Staff Witness Elizabeth Acosta

 4   Q.        What does Staff Witness Acosta recommend regarding the residential

 5             customer charger?

 6   A.        Ms. Acosta recommends limiting the residential customer charge to $9.50

 7             in 2027 and $12.00 in 2028. 22

 8   Q.        Do you agree with Ms. Acosta’s recommendation?

 9   A.        No. Ms. Acosta’s recommendation is lower than EPE’s proposed charges

10             of $14.56 and $19.17, 23 but it remains higher than the cost-based level the

11             record supports. A customer charge is paid every month regardless of how

12             much electricity a customer uses. As I explain above, those costs come to

13             $8.88 per month once the costs Mr. Barnes shows are not appropriately

14             characterized as customer charges and the service-line costs recorded in

15             FERC Account 369 are removed. Ms. Acosta’s $12.00 charge would

16             therefore recover an additional $3.12 per month, or $37.44 per year from


     22
               Elizabeth Acosta Direct Test. at 7:3–12 (Oct. 23, 2026).
     23
               Carrasco Direct Am. at 41:9–12.
                                                16
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        each residential customer for costs that are beyond the customer meter and

 2        part of the distribution system.

 3                 Ms. Acosta’s recommendation would also result in a substantially

 4        larger increase than the Commission has approved for this charge in prior

 5        EPE rate cases. The $7.00 charge was set by stipulation in EPE’s 2009 rate

 6        case, and the Commission retained it in Case No. 15-00127-UT, when EPE

 7        proposed $10.00, and again in EPE’s 2020 rate case, when EPE proposed

 8        $10.88. 24 Ms. Acosta’s $12.00 charge would increase the charge by 71

 9        percent. My recommended charge of $8.88 would increase it by 27 percent,

10        an increase limited to the amount supported by EPE’s customer-related

11        costs.

12                 A higher customer charge would also reduce customers’ ability to

13        manage their electricity bills. EPE states that the customer charge would

14        represent approximately 15 percent of base-rate charges, 25 but DOJ Witness

15        Mamkhezri recalculated that figure from EPE’s own rate design and found




     24
          Carrasco Direct Am. at 42:3–14.
     25
          Id. at 50:6–8.
                                             17
                    Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                    Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             that it is 17.85 percent. 26 Each dollar shifted into the customer charge is a

 2             dollar that customers cannot reduce through conservation and efficiency,

 3             and such a shift increases bills most for the customers who use the least

 4             electricity.

 5        d.        Response to Staff Witness Christopher E. Dunn

 6   Q.        What does Staff Witness Dunn state regarding LIR eligibility?

 7   A.        Mr. Dunn identifies limiting LIR eligibility to LIHEAP recipients as Staff’s

 8             position and provides a summary of Staff’s recommendations to limit

9              eligibility to LIHEAP. 27

10   Q.        Do you agree with Mr. Dunn’s statement?

11   A.        No. For the reasons I explain in response to Mr. Bunch, that limitation

12             would leave out most of the income-qualified households in EPE’s service

13             territory. Staff’s concern that broader eligibility would increase the cost of

14             the program 28 is answered by Staff’s own recommendation, which Mr.

15             Dunn identifies in the same summary, that the cost of the LIR be recovered


     26
               Jamal Mamkhezri Direct Test. at 10:195–98, tbl. JM-01 (Oct. 23, 2026)
     27
               Christopher E. Dunn Direct Test. at 7–8, tbl. CED-1, Item 12 (Oct. 23,
     2026).
     28
               Bunch Direct at 16:11–13.
                                                18
                    Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                                    Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1             from all customers. 29 When the cost is shared by all customer classes, the

 2             cost of reaching more eligible households is spread across EPE’s entire

 3             customer base, and there is no reason to hold eligibility to a level that Staff’s

 4             own data show reaches only about one in four eligible households.

 5        e.       Response to DOJ Witness Jamal Mamkhezri

 6   Q.        What does Dr. Mamkhezri recommend regarding the cost recovery of

 7             the LIR?

 8   A.        Dr. Mamkhezri recommends that the cost of the LIR be recovered only from

 9             other residential customers. 30 Dr. Mamkhezri supports EPE’s proposal to

10             recover the cost within the residential class and states that doing so keeps

11             the cost from spreading to non-residential classes, consistent with cost

12             causation. 31

13   Q.        Do you agree with Dr. Mamkhezri’s recommendation?

14   A.        No. The cost of the LIR should be paid by all customer classes. Low-income

15             rate relief carries out a statewide policy, the residential class does not cause



     29
               Dunn Direct at 7–8, tbl. CED-1, Item 12.
     30
               Mamkhezri Direct 12:237–240.
     31
               Id.
                                                  19
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                              Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        its cost, its benefits flow to the entire system, and charging it only to

 2        residential customers would place the cost on households that are

 3        themselves struggling. I disagree for four reasons.

 4               First, the Legislature made low-income rate relief a policy of the

 5        State without assigning its cost to any one class. The statute authorizes the

 6        Commission to approve rates and programs designed to reduce the burden

 7        of energy costs on low-income customers, but it does not prescribe how the

 8        cost of those rates is to be recovered. 32 A cost incurred to carry out a

 9        statewide policy objective is a cost of providing utility service in New

10        Mexico and should be borne by all of the customers who receive that

11        service.

12               Second, the residential class does not cause the cost of the LIR. Dr.

13        Mamkhezri’s cost-causation argument assumes that the residential class is

14        responsible for the cost, but no residential customer causes another

15        household’s inability to pay. As Staff Witness Bunch explains, the fact that

16        some residential customers struggle to pay their bills confers no



     32
          NMSA § 62-8-6(C); see Bunch Direct at 13:8–10.
                                           20
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        responsibility on better-off customers who happen to be in the same rate

 2        class. 33 The cost arises from the State’s policy decision and from EPE’s

 3        obligation to serve every customer in its territory, both of which are

 4        obligations of the system as a whole.

 5                Third, the benefits of the LIR flow to the entire system, and EPE

 6        already recovers from all classes the cost the LIR is designed to reduce. A

 7        program that helps low-income households keep up with their bills reduces

 8        uncollectible expense, lowers the cost of disconnecting and reconnecting

 9        service, and improves the stability of EPE’s revenue. 34 EPE allocates its

10        uncollectible expense among customer classes on the basis of revenue,

11        rather than assigning to each class only the uncollectibles its own customers

12        generate. 35 The non-residential classes therefore already pay a share of the

13        cost of residential non-payment. It would be inconsistent to spread the cost

14        of unpaid bills across all classes while assigning the cost of preventing those

15        unpaid bills to the residential class alone.



     33
          Bunch Direct at 14:8–13.
     34
          Id. at 15:9–13.
     35
          Id.
                                            21
               Rebuttal Testimony and Exhibits of Courtney Fieldman

                               Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1               Fourth, residential-only recovery places the cost on households that

 2        are themselves struggling. Mr. Bunch estimates that approximately 20,496

 3        of EPE’s New Mexico residential customers have incomes below the

 4        federal poverty level, 36 while EPE projects that 5,329 customers would

 5        receive the LIR. 37 Under Dr. Mamkhezri’s approach, roughly 15,000

 6        households below the poverty level that would not be enrolled would help

 7        pay for the credits received by those that are.

 8               Recovering the cost from all classes would roughly halve the burden

 9        on residential customers. Residential customers produce $73.1 million of

10        EPE’s $140.0 million in current New Mexico base revenue, or

11        approximately 52 percent. 38 EPE estimates that its proposed credit would
